h1: WSET wine qualifications compared, level by level
title: WSET Wine Levels Compared | Craft Beer School
desc: A plain guide to WSET Levels 1 to 4 in wine: what each covers, the exams, who each level suits and how to choose in India.
teaser: Level 1 or Level 2? Is the Diploma worth it? Here is what each WSET wine level asks of you and what it gives back.
standfirst: The Wine and Spirit Education Trust runs the best-known wine qualifications in the world. Each level suits a different reader, from the curious drinker to the future buyer. This guide compares them so you can pick a starting point.
sections:
The Wine and Spirit Education Trust (WSET) is a London based awarding body that sets syllabuses and exams in wine, spirits and sake. It does not usually teach every course itself. Approved programme providers run the classes and exams in cities around the world, including in India. Course dates, formats and fees are set by each provider, so compare a few before you book.

WSET also runs beer qualifications. If beer is your main interest, our guide to the WSET beer course covers that path.

A beginner course, often taught in a single day. You learn the main styles of wine, a handful of key grape varieties, how to taste and describe wine in a structured way and the basics of food and wine pairing and serving.

The exam is a short multiple choice paper. There is no blind tasting exam at this level.

Who it suits: anyone starting out, front of house staff, people moving into drinks sales and curious drinkers who want structure.

The level most people mean when they say they did WSET. It usually runs over several sessions or a few weeks with home study. You cover the main grape varieties, how climate and winemaking shape style and the major wine regions of the world, along with sparkling and fortified wines.

The exam is a multiple choice paper. It tests knowledge rather than tasting, though tasting is a big part of the classes.

Who it suits: restaurant and retail staff, people in distribution and marketing and serious enthusiasts. You can join at Level 2 without doing Level 1.

A big step up. You study why wines taste the way they do: vineyard choices, winemaking decisions and the commercial factors behind price and style. The tasting method becomes much more precise. You are expected to judge quality and readiness to drink.

The exam has a theory paper with multiple choice and short written answers, plus a blind tasting of two wines. Many students find the written answers the hardest part, because you have to explain causes, not list facts. Level 2 or equivalent knowledge is strongly recommended first.

Who it suits: sommeliers, buyers, wine educators, sales managers and anyone who wants a career in wine.

The Diploma is an expert level qualification taken over two years or more, in several separately examined units. It covers viticulture and winemaking in depth, the wine business, wines of the world, sparkling and fortified wines, with demanding blind tasting and essay papers.

It is a serious commitment of time and money. The study load sits alongside a full time job for most students. It is often seen as the stepping stone towards the Master of Wine, which is run by a separate body, the Institute of Masters of Wine.

Who it suits: people already working in wine who want to buy, teach, write or lead at a senior level.

• Just curious: Level 1, or go straight to Level 2 if you read a lot already.
  • Working in hospitality or sales: Level 2, then Level 3 when you want to move up.
  • Planning a wine career: Level 3, then the Diploma once you have a few years in the trade.

Be honest about what WSET teaches. It is about tasting, knowledge and the trade. It is not a winemaking course. It will not teach you to run a fermentation, manage a cellar or fix a stuck ferment. If you want to make wine, you need production training alongside it. Our brewing certifications guide makes the same distinction for beer, where tasting and making are separate skills too.

Indian students have extra hurdles. Many classic wines in the syllabus are expensive or hard to find here, so tasting practice costs more than it does in London. Join or form a tasting group to share bottles. Practise tasting at the right temperature, because a red served at 30 °C will mislead you on alcohol and structure.

Use Indian wines as practice too. Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc, Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon are widely grown here and appear on the syllabus.
faqs: Yes. You can join Level 2 directly. Many people do. Level 3 strongly recommends Level 2 or equivalent knowledge first.
Does WSET Level 3 have a tasting exam?
Yes. Level 3 includes a blind tasting of two wines alongside a theory paper with multiple choice and short written answers.
Is the WSET Diploma the same as Master of Wine?
No. The Diploma is WSET's Level 4 qualification. Master of Wine is a separate qualification run by the Institute of Masters of Wine.
Will WSET teach me to make wine?
No. WSET covers tasting, wine knowledge and the trade. For production skills you need a winemaking course alongside it.
